items.title: Yes to Life, in Spite of Everything: Viktor Frankl’s Lost Lectures on Moving Beyond Optimism and Pessimism to Find the Deepest Source of Meaning
items.description: "Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is... on each person... creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being."

items.title: Hannah Arendt on Love and How to Live with the Fundamental Fear of Loss
items.description: “Fearlessness is what love seeks… Such fearlessness exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”

items.title: The Only Three Distinctions Between People
items.description: It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. items.title: Roots and the Meaning of Life
items.description: They are so far out of sight for us, creatures of the upper world, that we don’t readily think of them. But as soon as we do, as soon as we plunge the mind into the cold dark humus to which the body will one day return, they become a spell against despair and a consecration of all that is alive. Beneath our feet, roots spread fractal and pulmonary, veining the biosphere with the bloodstream of life. items.title: How to Hold What Harrows You
items.description: We are shaped by all we have suffered — by what harrows us — and in turn shape our lives by how we hold our harrowing. Harrow shares its Middle English root with harvest. It is by suffering, and by what we make of our suffering, that our personhood ripens in us, that we come to reap what evolution sowed long ago when mitochondria first set out to become mind — our capacity for empathy, for doubt, for art. items.title: The Grasshopper and the “Lusory Attitude” Essential for Playing the Game of Life
items.description: On a recent flight, I watched a mother across the aisle play peek-a-boo with her small son while next to me a grown man in a VR headset spent six hours ascending the levels of a video game. It occurred to me that what I was doing between them — reading — was also a game: a peek-a-boo of ideas advancing across levels of meaning. items.title: Swimming and the Meaning of Life
items.description: One of my earliest and most vivid childhood memories is of swimming in a cool pool bounded by boulders in the middle of a river in the mountains of Bulgaria, the late-afternoon sun casting komorebi on the water through the rustling leaves. I can still hear the feeling-tone in my body, the strange and lovely simultaneity of absolute presence and absolute peace. I didn’t yet know the word for transcendence. items.title: Thank You, Everything: An Illustrated Love Letter to the World
items.description: We forget that none of this had to exist — that we weren’t owed mountains and music by the universe. And maybe we have to forget — or we would be too stupefied with gratitude for every raindrop and every eyelash to get through the daily tasks punctuating the unbidden wonder of our lives. items.title: What Makes You You Makes the Universe: Nobel Laureate Erwin Schrödinger on Quantum Physics, Vedanta, and the Ongoing Mystery of What We Are
items.description: "This life of yours which you are living is not merely a piece of the entire existence, but is in a certain sense the whole."

items.title: How to Live and How to Die
items.description: "Leave something of sweetness and substance in the mouth of the world."

items.title: Rilke on the Relationship Between Solitude, Love, Sex, and Creativity
items.description: "There is only one solitude, and it is large and not easy to bear... People are drawn to the easy and to the easiest side of the easy. But it is clear that we must hold ourselves to the difficult."

items.title: Trial, Triumph, and the Art of the Possible: The Remarkable Story Behind Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy”
items.description: A hymn of rage, a hymn of redemption, and a timeless love letter to the possible.

items.title: Polyvagal Theory and the Neurobiology of Connection: The Science of Rupture, Repair, and Reciprocity
items.description: "The mind narrates what the nervous system knows. Story follows state."

items.title: A Spell Against Stagnation: John O’Donohue on Beginnings
items.description: "Our very life here depends directly on continuous acts of beginning."

items.title: Enchantment and the Courage of Joy: René Magritte on the Antidote to the Banality of Pessimism
items.description: "Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, precisely because it is so easy to do so."
